1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5.name: Benoni Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5.background: The name goes back to Aaron Reinganum's 1825 book Ben-Oni, which analysed, among other openings, the then unknown 1.d4 c5. The Modern Benoni, with ...e6 after 3.d5, was introduced by Frank Marshall at New York 1927, revived by Soviet players in the 1950s and played by Mikhail Tal against Mikhail Botvinnik in their 1960 world championship match.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5.strategy: Pushes the attacked pawn past Black's and takes space, with c4 behind it as support. Black must now decide how and when to break the pawn chain, and that decision sets the character of the game, from a pawn sacrifice for queenside pressure to a sharp central imbalance.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3.name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Anti-Benoni Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends d4 with a developing move and steers clear of the Benoni's sharp pawn structures. If Black trades on d4, White recaptures with the knight and keeps a pawn on c4 that clamps d5; the price is the space and the cramping pawn that 3.d5 would have claimed.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3.strategy: Defends d4 solidly and opens the f1-bishop, but lets Black trade the less valuable c-pawn for White's central d-pawn. White gives up the chance of a space advantage and has to be content with a calm, level game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.dxc5.strategy: Takes a pawn that Black wins straight back: ...e6 opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and ...Bxc5 recovers it. White has traded the important d-pawn for Black's c-pawn and gained nothing for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.dxc5 e6.name: Benoni Defence: Weenink Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.dxc5 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal so that ...Bxc5 will win the pawn back, trading Black's flank pawn for White's central one. White cannot hold the extra pawn comfortably and has no advantage.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.dxc5 Na6.strategy: Regains the pawn with the knight on c5, which keeps the central pawns flexible and the e-pawn at home. The knight starts on the rim with no other job, though, and the f8-bishop stays shut in, so the pawn comes back at the price of a less harmonious development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.dxc5 Qa5+.strategy: Checks and wins the pawn back with the queen, so material is level again. The queen comes out very early, however, and White develops with a gain of time against it, so Black has little to show for the check.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6.strategy: Fianchettoes the bishop and keeps the option of trading on d4 for later. Solid and flexible, but it does not make use of the chance to trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 cxd4.strategy: Takes the chance the quiet 3.e3 offers: Black trades the c-pawn for White's central d-pawn at once, so White's centre loses its leading pawn and Black can strike in the centre in turn. White ends up with an isolated d-pawn or a plain, even game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 e6.strategy: Solid and flexible: it opens the f8-bishop and keeps both the trade on d4 and a central strike in reserve. It is slower than taking at once, and White keeps the choice between releasing the tension and entering a Benoni-type structure with d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3.strategy: The principal development: the knight guards d5 and e4 and keeps every set-up open, and it builds the compact position that 3.e3 aims for. It asks nothing of Black yet, but White loses nothing in flexibility and leaves Black to decide what to do about the c-pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight and adds a defender to d4, which the c-pawn presses. The set-up is compact and solid, and the game usually reaches the same positions as with the other knight first; White only decides later where the second knight goes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.d5.strategy: Gains space at once and cramps Black's pieces, but commits the d-pawn before White has developed. The pawn is supported only by c4 and the queen for now, and Black has the usual counterplay against an advanced pawn: the bishop on the long diagonal and play on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop on its natural diagonal and prepares to castle. It works from a distance: behind the knight on f6 it aims at White's centre, while the c-pawn already presses on d4. Black prefers pressure on the centre to occupying it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 cxd4.strategy: Trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn at once, so the exchange costs no time and the c-file opens for Black. White is left with a plain centre and no clear plan, and Black can challenge it. The cost is that Black gives up the tension on d4 that the bishop on g7 would build.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and keeps the d-pawn flexible, so Black can answer d5 by taking, or recapture on c5 with the bishop. It is a sound, quiet set-up, but it does not put pressure on White and leaves White the choice of structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight adds a defender to d4, which Black's c-pawn is pressing, and covers e5. White builds a compact, solid set-up and leaves it to Black whether to exchange on d4 or keep the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Nge.strategy: Develops the knight to e2, where it supports d4 and c3 and can recapture on d4 with a piece, while the f-pawn stays free. The price is that the f1-bishop is blocked until the knight moves or the long diagonal is opened with a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.d5.strategy: Gains space and fixes the centre, so the game turns into a closed fight in which White holds the space. White commits the d-pawn before the pieces are out, and Black has the usual counterplay against an advanced pawn on the queenside and on the long diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.e3 g6 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Nf3.strategy: Castles early, tucking the king behind the fianchettoed bishop and connecting the rooks. With the kingside settled, Black decides when to challenge d4 with the c-pawn, and White has not yet claimed more space than Black can contest.

Trades the c-pawn for White's central pawn at once, opening the c-file and removing the pawn that gives White's centre its space. Black delays castling for it and then has free play against whatever pawn or knight lands on d4.

A solid, flexible move that guards c5 and e5, but it leaves the decision to White. If White exchanges on c5 and Black recaptures with the d-pawn, the queens come off and Black can no longer castle, since the king has not yet moved to safety.

Completes the solid set-up: the bishop prepares castling and keeps the e3-d4 pawn chain intact. White aims at sound development and not space, and accepts that Black can challenge d4 at once, so the game stays level and depends on how White handles the centre after the exchange.

Takes space in the centre and cramps Black's pieces before Black has settled the c-pawn. White commits the d-pawn, and the game turns into a closed fight where Black strikes at the advanced pawn from the flank and down the long diagonal.

Prepares to develop the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, where it presses on the centre and on Black's kingside. It is a quiet, sound set-up, but it leaves Black free to trade on d4 and strike at the centre at once.

Trades the c-pawn for White's central d-pawn. It opens the c-file for Black's rook and leaves the d4 pawn a target for the fianchettoed bishop once the f6 knight steps aside. The exchange reduces White's control of the centre.

A waiting move that guards c5 and prepares to meet any advance in the centre. It leaves White the choice: White can exchange on c5 and trade queens into a level ending, or close the centre and gain space.

Develops the knight to hit d4 a second time and keeps the trade of the c-pawn in hand. It invites an advance of White's d-pawn that drives the knight to the edge, and then Black must fight the space White has gained.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4.strategy: Takes the d-pawn at once, exchanging Black's flank pawn for White's central one. The game takes a Sicilian-like character, with White's pawn on c4 where the Sicilian has one on e4, and Black gets a half-open c-file and a fair share of the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and keeps both the trade on d4 and a central strike in reserve. White can still enter the Benoni structure by pushing the d-pawn, or play quietly, so Black must be ready for both, but the move is solid and keeps the pawn structure intact.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 g6.strategy: Starts the fianchetto and puts off the decision about the c-pawn. The move is solid, but Black has not yet traded for White's central pawn, so White can keep the tension on White's own terms, by taking space or by releasing it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Recaptures with a developing move and puts the knight on a central post, where it eyes c6 and e6. White has traded a central pawn for a flank pawn, so the question is whether the knight can keep that post: Black can challenge it at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and delays the recapture. White still gets the pawn back, but Black has a free choice of set-up, including ...e5 to try to hold the pawn, and it is a slower way to recover it than the direct recapture.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.e3.strategy: Plans to win the pawn back on d4 with the e-pawn or the knight, and opens the queen's bishop. It is sound but slower than the direct recapture, and White's centre is less active than with a knight on d4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5.strategy: Kicks the knight away and takes space in the centre. The price is a hole on d6, which no black pawn guards any more, and the knight can aim for it. Black has to make up for that with quick development and activity.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e6.strategy: The natural development: it opens the f8-bishop and keeps a healthy structure with no weakened square, and the half-open c-file is Black's. White's knight can be challenged at once, and White has the lead in space but nothing more, so Black's game is comfortable and level.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nc6.strategy: Challenges the centre knight with a developing move. If White trades on c6, Black recaptures with the b-pawn, which takes control of d5 and opens the b-file, at the price of an isolated a-pawn. A natural, sound way to put the knight to the test at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..strategy: The most active retreat: the knight, protected by the c-pawn, eyes the hole on d6 and the squares c7 and a7 instead of falling back passively. It stands far from the kingside, though, and Black can strike at once in the centre.
The safe retreat: the knight keeps out of trouble and covers c5 and a5 from b3. But it is passive, and Black takes the centre at once and develops with the initiative.
Falls back to c2, where the knight covers d4 and e3 and is out of reach. It has no future there and blocks the queen's diagonal, and Black takes the centre at once and develops with ease.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..name: English Opening: Symmetrical Variation, Anti-Benoni Variation, Kasparov-Vaganian Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.Nf3 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5 5..strategy: Strikes in the centre at once and offers the d-pawn. White's knight is offside, and Black plays for quick development and active pieces in return for the pawn.

Puts the question to the knight at once: Nd6+ would simply lose it to the bishop, so it must retreat, and Black gains a tempo and a useful queenside pawn move. The move does not develop a piece or fight for the centre, though, and the knight returns with a healthy game.

Defends e5 with a pawn and keeps the structure solid, but gives up the central strike. With the c-pawn gone, d5 is a square Black's pawns cannot easily contest, so White's pieces can settle there, and Black gets a safe but passive position.
